Description: Carbon plays a key role in the physical and chemical evolution of the universe. carbon species are important gas coolants in both diffuse and dense clouds, and the majority of complex molecules in the interstellar medium (ism) are made of carbon, with the most complex being carbonaceous dust in the solid state. more significantly, carbon-based chemistry is central to the origin of life. SOLAR system objects show systematic variations in their carbon abundances carbon in comets is similar to that in the ism while meteorites are depleted in carbon (relative to silicon) BY an order of magnitude relative to the sun and the ism (e.g., pontoppidan et AL. 2014). meteorite and comet analyses, studies of carbon dust (jones et AL. 2016), and observations of young protoplanetary disks (e.g., bergin et AL. 2016) imply possible evidence for carbon cycling from the gas to solid phases in the early evolution of the SOLAR nebula. here, we focus on the evolution of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (pahs) a ubiquitous component of the ism constituting   20% of all available carbon and one of its most stable forms. carbon in meteorites is mostly in the form of organics (alexander 2011), including aromatic materials such AS small pahs (c<24), suggesting the large pahs (c>30) of the ism could survive AS condensates in disks and serve AS the chemical feedstock of SOLAR system organics. the recognition that pahs condense onto icy grains in cold regions under many astrophysical situations has LED to a slew of experiments studying pahs in ices (e.g., bernstein et AL. 1999, gudipati & allamandola 2003, bouwman et AL. 2011, cuylle et AL. 2014, cook et AL. 2015). water ice lowers the ionization potential of pahs, facilitating PAH ion formation in the presence of UV and PAH destruction via chemical degradation processes, perhaps ultimately leading to the observed SOLAR system organics. we plan to investigate the role of PAH-water ice chemistry in an evolving nebula, with new laboratory experiments designed to closely replicate conditions across the entire planet-forming zone, from NEAR the snowline at a few AU to cold regions beyond the kuiper belt. thermochemical and dynamical disk models will guide experimental parameters such AS densities, temperatures and strength of UV radiation fields. fourier-transform infrared (ftir) and raman spectroscopy of various sized pahs (16-50 c atoms) isolated in a water ice matrix and irradiated BY UV photons, will determine both breakdown (degradation) rates and the resulting photoproducts this information will be assimilated into the NASA ames PAH IR spectroscopic database providing a rich legacy for future work on organics to be probed BY SOLAR system missions (e.g., icy worlds, mars 2020) and telescope facilities (e.g. jwst). the PAH destruction rate on ices determined from the experiments will be incorporated into disk evolution models to examine the possible survival of pahs AS condensates/complex organics on disks and quantify this mode of delivery of carbon to the inner disk.

Description: We propose to provide an organized, documented, and transparent archive of planetary mission data for the science community and general public worldwide through the continued operation of NASA's Planetary Data System (PDS) atmospheres node at new mexico state university. the atmospheres node (atm) will maximize NASA's return on its investment in planetary exploration and will aid in the expansion of knowledge of all communities. our team is uniquely qualified to provide this service to the planetary science community due to our collective expertise in planetary atmospheres, our role in the development of pds4, our history in working with missions and individual data providers, and our proposed initiatives for improving data discoverability and interoperability. the mission data we will curate in the atmospheres node (atm) consist of historical data already in the atm archive, data from current missions that are actively archiving at atm, and data from future missions with at least one instrument that will yield atmospheric science data. the historical and current mission data comprise an archive approximately 38 TB in size, arising from missions to every planet in the SOLAR system and acquired over a time period of more than 40 years. the future data we will archive will likely double the size of the atmos holdings and will be provided BY MRO, MAVEN, curiosity, insight, juno, perseverance, europa clipper, and atmospheric components of yet To Be Determined discovery and/or new frontiers missions. in addition, we will archive a range of ground-based telescopic, laboratory, and field data acquired in support of NASA missions AS well AS a variety of derived or higher order data products. in addition to the ongoing work with current and future mission teams, the other primary atmospheres node activities for the proposed award period will include: - migrating the atm data holdings that remain in pds3 to the more modern pds4 standards - working with individual data providers to efficiently archive their data products - expanding the development of the educational labeling system at atmospheres, a pds4 label template generator, to include a broader range of filetypes - obtaining dois for all atm data holdings to improve their citability and discoverability - developing and implementing a cloud computing strategy for atm that is aligned with PDS cloud computing roadmap - working with an external entity on atm website design and management - ensuring that the atm it systems are secure while maintaining data integrity in the atm archives - enhancing communication with our user community and ensuring accessibility of the atm data archives

Description: Motivation and science objectives: for billions of years, wind-driven erosion, transport, and deposition of sand and dust have shaped the surface of mars, generating a diversity of aeolian landscapes across the planet. these landscapes CAN provide key information about prevailing environmental conditions (both ancient and modern), assuming we have robust understanding of how atmospheric processes control aeolian activity on mars. AS new discoveries have challenged terrestrially-derived notions, it has become clear that we currently DO not have a firm grasp on how environmental parameters (e.g., gravity and atmospheric density) impact the dynamics of sediment transport. a mechanistic understanding of aeolian transport is crucial for deciphering the martian rock record, estimating erosion rates, validating and improving climate models, and mitigating risk to landed instruments and future human explorers. robotic surface missions, particularly those with joint meteorological and high-resolution imaging capabilities, provide rare opportunities to study aeolian surface activity in situ. within jezero crater, the future landing site of the mars 2020 rover, wind streaks, yardangs, and transverse aeolian ridges (tars) indicate multiple generations of aeolian activity. our investigation seeks to characterize the ancient and modern wind regimes within jezero crater, and in so doing achieve a better understanding of the dynamics of aeolian transport under differing environmental conditions while also supporting the mission's primary science objectives. this work will build upon similar studies LED BY the PI AS PART of the MSL and insight missions and will include three primary science objectives: objective 1: characterize the modern surface environment. change detection experiments conducted from the mars 2020 rover cameras (e.g., mastcam-z) will be used to monitor aeolian activity on the surface. these observations will help identify formative wind patterns and characterize seasonal and diurnal variations in surface activity. concurrent imaging and atmospheric monitoring from the mars environmental dynamics analyzer (meda) instrument will also allow us to constrain motion thresholds on mars and probe the relationship between wind speed and sediment flux. objective 2: decipher paleoclimatic conditions in jezero crater. color and STEREO imaging of paleofeatures encountered along the rover s traverse will provide valuable insight into ancient climatic conditions within the crater. in particular, mastcam-z and watson images of features such AS ventifacts, cross-bedded sandstones and transverse aeolian ridges (tars) CAN provide vital information about prior episodes of aeolian activity and the environmental conditions (e.g., wind speed, atmospheric density, wind direction) driving this activity. objective 3: support high-priority science activities. change detection imaging will be conducted during major scientific campaigns (e.g., mars helicopter technology demonstrator flights and drilling/sampling activities). these images will aid in scientific interpretation of collected material and will also help mitigate risk to rover instruments (particularly those placed in close contact with the surface). regular deck monitoring images will also document accumulation and removal of wind-blown material on rover hardware, including around the MOXIE inlet.
